subtitle: Line up flip-flops and you can store a word, shift it, or count with it.

reg.body: One flip-flop remembers one bit. Want to remember a whole number? Line them up. An n-bit register is n D flip-flops sharing one clock: on each clock edge all bits load in parallel. A load-enable input decides whether the register takes new data or holds. Registers are how a CPU keeps values between steps. A 16-bit register needs one flip-flop per bit, so 16 of them. Without a load-enable, a register built from D flip-flops would reload new data on every clock edge and could never hold a value.
keynotes: An n-bit register is n D flip-flops sharing one clock: on each clock edge all bits load in parallel.
A load-enable input decides whether the register takes new data or holds.
A 16-bit register needs 16 flip-flops, one per bit.

shift.body:
Now connect them in a line, like people passing a bucket. Connect each flip-flop’s Q to the next one’s D: on every clock edge the word shifts one place. Serial-in/serial-out delays data by n clocks; serial-in/parallel-out turns a bit stream into a word (and the reverse converts parallel to serial, used in UART/SPI). Shifting left multiplies by 2; right divides by 2.

Shift 1011 left by one, with a new bit 0: you get 0110, the old top bit dropped, so the value doubles in effect. In the figure a bit entered now comes out four clocks later: a 4-bit serial-in serial-out shift register delays a bit by four clocks.
keynotes: Connecting each flip-flop’s Q to the next one’s D shifts the word one place on every clock edge.
Serial-in/serial-out delays data by n clocks; serial-in/parallel-out turns a bit stream into a word (UART/SPI).
Shifting left multiplies by 2 and shifting right divides by 2.

async.body:
Here is a counter you can build with almost no thought. Chain T flip-flops (T = 1) so each one clocks the next: the first toggles every clock, the second every two, and so on, and the outputs count in binary. An n-bit counter has 2ⁿ states and its top bit runs at f/2ⁿ.

Try it: a 4-bit counter clocked at 1600 Hz has its top bit Q3 at 1600 ÷ 2⁴ = 100 Hz. The drawback is that the change ripples through, so outputs briefly show wrong values (glitches) and the max clock is limited by the delay of n stages. In the figure Q0 is half the clock, Q1 a quarter, and so on. An n-bit binary counter has 2ⁿ states.
keynotes: Chained T flip-flops (T = 1) each clock the next, so the outputs count in binary.
An n-bit counter has 2ⁿ states and its top bit runs at f/2ⁿ: a 4-bit counter at 1600 Hz has Q3 at 100 Hz.
Drawback: the change ripples through, so outputs briefly show wrong values (glitches) and the max clock is limited by the delay of n stages.

sync.body: Can we count without the ripple? Yes, if you make every flip-flop listen to the same clock. In a synchronous counter every flip-flop shares the clock and logic decides which toggle: bit k toggles when all lower bits are 1. No ripple, so it is faster and glitch-free, at the cost of a few AND gates. Up/down counting just changes that logic. Why is a synchronous counter faster than a ripple counter? Because all bits change together instead of waiting for each other in turn.
keynotes: In a synchronous counter every flip-flop shares the clock and logic decides which toggle: bit k toggles when all lower bits are 1.
There is no ripple, so it is faster and glitch-free, at the cost of a few AND gates.
Up/down counting just changes that logic.

modn.body:
What if you need to count to 10, or to 60 for seconds on a clock? A binary counter naturally counts to a power of two, so you cut it short. To count 0…N−1, detect the state N and immediately reset (asynchronous clear) or load 0 (synchronous). A decade (mod-10) counter detects 1010 (10) and resets to 0000. The number of flip-flops needed is n = ⌈log₂ N⌉.

For a mod-60 counter for seconds: 2⁵ = 32 < 60 ≤ 64 = 2⁶, so six flip-flops. A mod-10 counter needs at least four flip-flops.
keynotes: To count 0…N−1, detect the state N and reset (asynchronous clear) or load 0 (synchronous).
A decade (mod-10) counter detects 1010 (10) and resets to 0000.
The number of flip-flops needed is n = ⌈log₂ N⌉, so a mod-60 counter needs six.

ring.body:
Two clever counters need no decoding logic at all. A ring counter circulates a single 1 round an n-bit shift register: n states, and each state is decoded by one bit. A Johnson (twisted-ring) counter feeds back the inverted last output, giving 2n states with the same flip-flops.

Follow a 4-bit Johnson counter from 0000: 0000 → 1000 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → 0001 → 0000. That is 8 states from 4 flip-flops, so an n-bit Johnson counter has 2n states.
keynotes: A ring counter circulates a single 1 round an n-bit shift register: n states, each decoded by one bit.
A Johnson (twisted-ring) counter feeds back the inverted last output, giving 2n states with the same flip-flops.
A 4-bit Johnson counter from 0000 has 8 states.
